note.label: From Milk to Meat: Train All Your Senses

precepts.why:
Moses commanded: “thou shalt read this law before all Israel in their hearing.” In their hearing. “Gather the people together, men, and women, and children, and thy stranger that is within thy gates, that they may hear, and that they may learn, and fear the Lord your God, and observe to do all the words of this law”. Faith comes by hearing, and hearing by the word of God: in hearing we process what we heard, learn from it, and apply it to our life.

So we have to exercise these senses: in what we watch, as Job 31 was pulled up, and in our hearing, what we ingest and listen to. “Be not deceived: evil communications corrupt good manners.” What you digest in your vision and your hearing will change the way you think.

That is why the law is read in the hearing of the whole house, even “their children, which have not known any thing”, so that they may hear and learn to fear the Lord. If the ear is filled with the law, it forms the mind in the law; if it is filled with evil communications, it corrupts the manners.

We exercise the physical senses, what we see and what we hear, so we can tap into the spiritual senses we have. Going from milk to meat means training the ear on the word of God and guarding it from everything that would corrupt it.

precepts.text: Ye shall soon utterly perish from off the land; and the Lord shall scatter you among the nations, and ye shall be left few in number among the heathen. Moses saw the Israelites scattered throughout the four corners of the earth.
precepts.point: For I know that after my death ye will utterly corrupt yourselves, and turn aside from the way which I have commanded you; and evil will befall you in the latter days. Moses saw the latter days. Why can Moses say I know? Because God showed Moses what would happen to us: in the time of the Babylonians, the Greeks, the Romans, and here in America.

note.label: Passover Class: Exodus From America Modern Day Egypt

precepts.why:
In Deuteronomy 31 Moses says, “For I know that after my death ye will utterly corrupt yourselves”, and “evil will befall you in the latter days”. How is Moses able to say I know? Deuteronomy 4 shows what he saw.

“I call heaven and earth to witness against you this day, that ye shall soon utterly perish from off the land whereunto ye go over Jordan to possess it; ye shall not prolong your days upon it, but shall utterly be destroyed.” When we went into the land of Israel, our days were not going to be prolonged in it; we were going to be destroyed from off that land. “And the Lord shall scatter you among the nations, and ye shall be left few in number among the heathen, whither the Lord shall lead you.” Moses saw the Israelites being scattered throughout the four corners of the earth.

He could see it because God showed it to him. In 2 Esdras 14, read right after, the Lord says, “In the bush I did manifestly reveal myself unto Moses, and talked with him, when my people served in Egypt”, and he held him on the mount a long season, the forty days and forty nights, and “shewed him the secrets of the times, and the end”. Moses saw the secrets of the beginning, which is how he wrote Genesis, and he saw the end.

So Moses saw what would happen to us in the time of the Babylonians, the Greeks and the Romans, and he saw us here in America, in the transatlantic slave trade, and America being destroyed. That is why he could say with certainty that evil would befall us in the latter days: he had already seen it.

precepts.text: At the end of every seven years, in the year of release, read the law at the feast of tabernacles.
precepts.point: A Hebrew servant goes free in the seventh year and is furnished liberally from the flock, the floor and the winepress.

note.label: Jubilee: The Year To Be Set Free

precepts.why:
“At the end of every seven years, in the solemnity of the year of release, in the feast of tabernacles”. Moses ties the year of release to a set time: every seventh year, in the feast of tabernacles. In that solemnity the land was released, the servants were released, and the debt was released.

It comes right after the Sabbath of the land in Leviticus 25. When the people ask, “What shall we eat the seventh year? behold, we shall not sow, nor gather in our increase”, God answers, “Then I will command my blessing upon you in the sixth year, and it shall bring forth fruit for three years.” Think about that with the seventh day Sabbath. Brothers and sisters say, I have to work on the Sabbath because that is my money day; that is the same question as verse 20, and it shows you do not believe what was read. Work six days and rest on the Sabbath, and the Most High will provide.

Deuteronomy 15:1 then goes into more detail on what that year of release in Deuteronomy 31:10 is: “At the end of every seven years thou shalt make a release”, and every creditor that lends to his neighbour, his brother, shall release it, “because it is called the Lord’s release.” Lend something, and at the end of seven years that debt is taken care of.

precepts.text: Make no marriages with the nations of the land, but destroy their altars and burn their graven images with fire.
precepts.point: Be strong and of a good courage, fear not, for the Most High goes with thee; he will not fail thee, nor forsake thee.

note.label: Deuteronomy 31: Moses' Final Charge and the Rebellion Foretold

precepts.why:
“The Lord thy God, he will go over before thee, and he will destroy these nations from before thee, and thou shalt possess them: and Joshua, he shall go over before thee”. The Most High himself goes over before Israel, and Joshua before the people, and he does to these nations “as he did to Sihon and to Og, kings of the Amorites”. Then: “the Lord shall give them up before your face, that ye may do unto them according unto all the commandments which I have commanded you.”

Which commandments? The guidelines of Deuteronomy 7 for when you enter the land: “Neither shalt thou make marriages with them; thy daughter thou shalt not give unto his son, nor his daughter shalt thou take unto thy son. For they will turn away thy son from following me, that they may serve other gods: so will the anger of the Lord be kindled against you, and destroy thee suddenly.” Do not take their daughters for wives or give your sons to theirs, and do not worship their gods.

“But thus shall ye deal with them; ye shall destroy their altars, and break down their images, and cut down their groves, and burn their graven images with fire.” Utterly burn their gods with fire. The nations are given up before Israel's face so that Israel may do exactly this to them. And the charge that goes with it: “Be strong and of a good courage, fear not, nor be afraid of them: for the Lord thy God, he it is that doth go with thee; he will not fail thee, nor forsake thee.”

precepts.text: Gather yourselves together, yea, gather together, O nation not desired.
precepts.point: Their children which have not known any thing must hear and learn to fear the Most High. The first thing you establish with your children, before they know anything else, is who they are and who their God is.

note.label: Deuteronomy 31: Moses' Final Charge and the Rebellion Foretold

precepts.why:
Moses wrote this law and delivered it to the priests, the sons of Levi that bear the ark of the covenant, and to all the elders of Israel, with a command: “At the end of every seven years, in the solemnity of the year of release, in the feast of tabernacles”, when all Israel is come to appear before the Lord, “thou shalt read this law before all Israel in their hearing.” The law had to be taught over and over, to remind the people what would befall them and what they must do.

“Gather the people together, men, and women, and children, and thy stranger that is within thy gates, that they may hear, and that they may learn, and fear the Lord your God, and observe to do all the words of this law”. Zephaniah gives the same call: “Gather yourselves together, yea, gather together, O nation not desired”. Israel, the nation not desired, is to gather to hear and learn the law, the same gathering as at the feast of tabernacles.

“And that their children, which have not known any thing, may hear, and learn to fear the Lord your God”. The first thing you establish with your children, before they know anything else, is who they are and who their God is.

precepts.text: If thou wilt not hearken to observe all his commandments, all these curses shall come upon thee.
precepts.point: You wonder where the Most High was when our babies were used as alligator bait, when we were packed on ships, hung, burnt, and raped in front of our own. His face was hid, because when he would have dwelt among us we went a whoring after other gods, so he left us in the hands of the people that hate us.

note.label: Deuteronomy 31: Moses' Final Charge and the Rebellion Foretold

precepts.why:
The Most High tells Moses his days approach that he must die, and to call Joshua to the tabernacle to receive his charge, and he appears in the pillar of a cloud over the door of the tabernacle. Then he tells Moses straight out: “Behold, thou shalt sleep with thy fathers; and this people will rise up, and go a whoring after the gods of the strangers of the land, whither they go to be among them, and will forsake me, and break my covenant which I have made with them.” The people Moses spent forty years tending will forsake the covenant. Instead of utterly destroying the nations and their gods, they will mingle with the nations and serve their gods.

“Then my anger shall be kindled against them in that day, and I will forsake them, and I will hide my face from them, and they shall be devoured, and many evils and troubles shall befall them”. Those many evils and troubles are the curses we just read through in Deuteronomy 28: “if thou wilt not hearken unto the voice of the Lord thy God, to observe to do all his commandments and his statutes which I command thee this day; that all these curses shall come upon thee, and overtake thee”. Going a whoring after other gods is not hearkening to his voice, and all these curses are the evils that befall.

You wonder where the Most High was when our babies were used as alligator bait, when we were packed on ships, hung, burnt and raped in front of our own. His face was hid: “I will surely hide my face in that day for all the evils which they shall have wrought, in that they are turned unto other gods.” When he would have dwelt among us, we went a whoring after other gods, so he left us in the hands of the people that hate us. That is why we say in that day, “Are not these evils come upon us, because our God is not among us?”

precepts.text: The Most High himself said, I have seen this people, and, behold, it is a stiffnecked people.
precepts.point: Israel became a burden to Moses to the point he asked the Most High to kill him rather than let him see his own wretchedness. While I am yet alive with you this day, ye have been rebellious against the Lord; and how much more after my death?

note.label: Deuteronomy 31: Moses' Final Charge and the Rebellion Foretold

precepts.why:
“For I know thy rebellion, and thy stiff neck”. A stiff neck means you are told what to do and you refuse to do it. If anybody knew Israel's rebellion, Moses knew, and the Most High himself said the same at the golden calf: “I have seen this people, and, behold, it is a stiffnecked people”.

Israel kept that spirit even after judgments, miracles and harsh consequences. Moses saw it for forty years, so he could say “while I am yet alive with you this day, ye have been rebellious against the Lord; and how much more after my death?”

precepts.text: Some when they had heard did provoke, and he was grieved with them forty years in the wilderness.
precepts.point: Israel became a burden to Moses to the point he asked the Most High to kill him rather than let him see his own wretchedness. While I am yet alive with you this day, ye have been rebellious against the Lord; and how much more after my death?

note.label: Deuteronomy 31: Moses' Final Charge and the Rebellion Foretold

precepts.why:
“For some, when they had heard, did provoke: howbeit not all that came out of Egypt by Moses. But with whom was he grieved forty years? was it not with them that had sinned, whose carcases fell in the wilderness?” All forty years in the wilderness Moses was grieved. Every day there was some issue, some drama the children of Israel raised, and the ones that provoked left their carcases in the wilderness.

We think we grieve dealing with a congregation of a few hundred. Moses dealt with the rebellious spirits of all twelve tribes, thousands upon thousands, for forty years. That is why he could say I know thy rebellion and thy stiff neck: ye have been rebellious against the Lord while I am yet alive, and how much more after my death?

precepts.text: Moses' grief: wherefore hast thou afflicted thy servant, the burden of all this people is too heavy for me; kill me, I pray thee, and let me not see my wretchedness.
precepts.point: Israel became a burden to Moses to the point he asked the Most High to kill him rather than let him see his own wretchedness. While I am yet alive with you this day, ye have been rebellious against the Lord; and how much more after my death?

note.label: Deuteronomy 31: Moses' Final Charge and the Rebellion Foretold

precepts.why:
Israel became such a burden to Moses that he asked the Most High to kill him: “Wherefore hast thou afflicted thy servant? and wherefore have I not found favour in thy sight, that thou layest the burden of all this people upon me? Have I conceived all this people? have I begotten them, that thou shouldest say unto me, Carry them in thy bosom, as a nursing father beareth the sucking child”. They wept to him for flesh to eat, and “I am not able to bear all this people alone, because it is too heavy for me.”

Then: “And if thou deal thus with me, kill me, I pray thee, out of hand, if I have found favour in thy sight; and let me not see my wretchedness.” That is the grief of forty years with a stiffnecked people. When Moses says “I know thy rebellion, and thy stiff neck”, he knew it well enough to have begged for death rather than see his own wretchedness under it.

precepts.text: On Sinai the Most High told Moses many wondrous things and showed him the secrets of the times and the end.
precepts.point: How did Moses know what would happen to the rebellious Israelites in the latter days? The Most High did not only give Moses the ten commandments on Sinai; he told him many wondrous things and showed him the secrets of the times. That is how Moses wrote Genesis, and that is how he saw ahead of time our people going into captivity again by slave ships, as Deuteronomy 28:68 declares. The prophecies of chapters 32 and 33 are still unfolding to this very day.

note.label: Deuteronomy 31: Moses' Final Charge and the Rebellion Foretold

precepts.why:
“For I know that after my death ye will utterly corrupt yourselves, and turn aside from the way which I have commanded you; and evil will befall you in the latter days”. This is heavy: Moses tells the elders and officers gathered before him that evil shall befall the people he is speaking to in the latter days, the last days, because they would do evil in the sight of the Lord and provoke him through the work of their hands. How did Moses know what would happen to the rebellious Israelites in the latter days?

Ezra answers it. The Most High did not only give Moses the ten commandments on Sinai: “I sent him and led my people out of Egypt, and brought him up to the mount of where I held him by me a long season, And told him many wondrous things, and shewed him the secrets of the times, and the end”. He held Moses by him a long season, told him many wondrous things, and showed him the secrets of the times and the end.

That is how Moses wrote Genesis, and that is how he saw ahead of time our people going into captivity again by slave ships, as Deuteronomy 28:68 declares. He could call heaven and earth to record against Israel because he had been shown the end. The prophecies of chapters 32 and 33 are still unfolding to this very day.
